flashcard_questions.q: When did Typhoon Haiyan strike the Philippines?
What category was Typhoon Haiyan on the Saffir-Simpson scale?
What sustained wind speeds did Typhoon Haiyan reach?
Which Philippine city was among the worst affected by Typhoon Haiyan?
How many people did Typhoon Haiyan kill?
How did most of Typhoon Haiyan's victims die?
flashcard_questions.a: They drowned in a 5-metre storm surge.

flashcard_questions.q: How many people did Typhoon Haiyan leave homeless?
How much did the price of rice rise after Typhoon Haiyan?
How many people were evacuated before Typhoon Haiyan made landfall?
How much aid money was raised for the Philippines after Typhoon Haiyan?
What was the aim of the Philippine 'Build Back Better' programme?
flashcard_questions.a: To rebuild homes and infrastructure to withstand future storms.

flashcard_questions.q: Which trees were replanted along the coast as a natural storm barrier?
Why can tropical storms be predicted when earthquakes cannot?
flashcard_questions.a: They form over the ocean and take days to reach land.

flashcard_questions.q: Why did many people in Tacloban ignore the warning about Haiyan?
flashcard_questions.a: They expected a minor Category 1 storm, not a Category 5.

flashcard_questions.q: What do roof straps do in a storm-protected building?
flashcard_questions.a: They tie the roof to the walls so it is not blown off.

notes: 15 cards: 9 case-study-to-fact with one figure each (November 2013, Category 5, 315 km/h, 6,300 dead, 4.1 million homeless, 12% rice rise, 800,000 evacuated, $89 million, 5-metre surge), 3 strategy-to-example (Build Back Better, mangroves, roof straps), 3 cause-to-consequence (why storms are predictable, the ignored warning, drowning in the surge). Dropped the primary/secondary effect definitions, which restate lesson headings, and the 1 million destroyed homes figure, which overlaps the homelessness card.
